title: SQL: understanding the result
lead: Learn SQL by working out the result table before running the statement.
goals: Work through WHERE, GROUP BY, and HAVING step by step
Distinguish inner and outer joins and calculate their result sizes
Use IN and EXISTS with small datasets

sections.title: The conceptual framework
sections.html:
SQL describes the desired result, such as “total sales by city”. The optimiser chooses an execution plan to compute that result. SQL normally uses bag semantics: duplicate rows remain unless duplicate elimination is requested with DISTINCT.

This lecture covers ORDER BY/LIMIT, aggregates such as SUM, GROUP BY/HAVING, joins that combine data, and subqueries nested within another query. To calculate results yourself, follow the logical order FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT. This order explains the statement’s meaning; it does not require the DBMS to execute the physical operations in that sequence.

DDL, DML and access control

DDL defines or changes schema objects; DML reads and changes the current data instance; DCL manages access privileges. Defining a table differs from inserting its rows. A query describes its result, while the DBMS can select a result-preserving execution algorithm.

Source topics: Physical PDF pp. 6, 7, 8 ↗. The worked examples are original.

sections.title: An original dataset and query
sections.html:
Let Sale(id, city, amount) contain (1, Hanoi, 40), (2, Hanoi, 70), (3, Hue, 30), (4, Hue, 90), (5, Hue, 10). Each row represents a sale; id identifies it, city names the city, and amount is measured in the same monetary unit. Find cities whose total exceeds 100, counting only sales of at least 30.

SELECT city, SUM(amount) AS total
FROM Sale
WHERE amount >= 30
GROUP BY city
HAVING SUM(amount) > 100
ORDER BY total DESC, city ASC;
  1. FROM provides five sales. WHERE examines individual rows and removes id=5 because 10 < 30, leaving ids 1, 2, 3, 4.
  2. GROUP BY groups the remaining rows by city: Hanoi has amounts 40, 70; Hue has 30, 90.
  3. SUM adds the values within each group: Hanoi has 40+70=110; Hue has 30+90=120. HAVING retains both because each total is > 100.
  4. SELECT returns city and names the sum total. ORDER BY sorts total in descending order, using ascending city order to break ties. The result is (Hue,120), (Hanoi,110).

Now change WHERE to amount > 50: only id=2 and id=4 remain, so the totals are 70 and 90. HAVING rejects both groups and the final result is empty.

Key takeaway

WHERE filters rows before aggregation; HAVING filters groups after aggregation. Changing WHERE changes which numbers enter SUM. Changing HAVING only determines whether an already-computed group appears.

sections.title: Joins and subqueries: an experiment with answers
sections.html:
A new dataset. Member(mid,name) = {(1,An),(2,Binh),(3,Chi)}; Borrow(mid,book) = {(1,A),(1,B),(2,C)}. The member identifier mid connects the tables; M and B below are table aliases.

SELECT M.name, B.book
FROM Member M LEFT JOIN Borrow B ON M.mid=B.mid
ORDER BY M.mid, B.book;

An matches two Borrow rows with mid=1, producing (An,A) and (An,B). Binh matches one row, producing (Binh,C). Chi matches none, but LEFT JOIN preserves this member and fills the Borrow side with NULL. The result is (An,A), (An,B), (Binh,C), (Chi,NULL). An inner join returns only the first three rows.

Key takeaway

One left-hand row can produce several result rows. A join produces one row for every matching pair. LEFT JOIN adds a NULL-padded row only when no match exists; it does not limit each member to one row.

SELECT M.name FROM Member M
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Borrow B WHERE B.mid=M.mid)
ORDER BY M.mid;

EXISTS asks only whether at least one loan exists. An and Binh have loans; Chi does not, so the result is An, Binh. An’s two loans still make the condition true just once for An’s Member row. With this NULL-free dataset, replacing the condition with M.mid IN (SELECT B.mid FROM Borrow B) gives the same result: IN tests whether the identifier appears in the list 1,1,2.

These queries serve different purposes: the join retrieves individual loans, while EXISTS retrieves members who have loans. Do not use one query’s row count as the answer for the other.

Extend the outer-join fixture with an orphan

Original fixture: Member has (1, An), (2, Binh), (3, Chi). Borrow has (1, A), (1, B), (2, C), and an added orphan (4, D), where the first field is member_id. No foreign-key constraint is enforced in this fixture; otherwise the orphan could be rejected. Join on Member.member_id = Borrow.member_id.

LEFT JOIN returns four rows: An/A, An/B, Binh/C, Chi/NULL. RIGHT JOIN returns four rows: An/A, An/B, Binh/C, NULL/D. FULL OUTER JOIN returns all five rows. The unmatched row is padded on the missing side, and An still has two matches; an outer join does not remove join multiplicity.

Exercise: why is the full join not six rows?

Worked answer. There are three matched pairs, one unmatched Member, and one unmatched Borrow. Count each matched pair once: 3 + 1 + 1 = 5.

Source topics: Physical PDF pp. 23, 24, 25 ↗. The worked examples are original.

sections.title: Independent practice and scope
sections.html:
On Sale, SELECT city returns 5 rows; SELECT DISTINCT city returns 2 values. Write a query that returns the highest-value sale, adding id to ORDER BY to resolve ties when several rows have the same amount.

A suggested answer
SELECT id, city, amount FROM Sale
ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC LIMIT 1;

The result is (4,Hue,90).

ALL/ANY are also introduced on PDF page 28. For the set {30,90}, 50 > ANY is true and 50 > ALL is false. This example contains no NULL values. NULL’s three-valued logic, TRUE, FALSE, UNKNOWN, needs supplementary reading; it cannot be inferred from an outer-join diagram.

Read these points together: slide 14 simplifies where aggregates can occur, but slide 18 shows an aggregate in HAVING. A correlated subquery can be understood row by row, although the optimiser may transform its execution.

Negative queries, NULL and empty quantified comparisons

A correlated NOT EXISTS query keeps a Member when no Borrow row has the same member_id. In the non-NULL fixture above it returns Chi. NOT IN gives the same result only under suitable non-NULL assumptions. With SQL NULL, a comparison may be UNKNOWN, and WHERE retains only TRUE. The expression 2 NOT IN (1, NULL) is UNKNOWN: neither comparison proves that 2 differs from every element.

For equality comparisons, IN corresponds to = ANY and NOT IN to <> ALL. An empty ANY is false; an empty ALL is true. If no decisive true comparison exists for ANY, or no decisive false comparison exists for ALL, a NULL comparison can make the result UNKNOWN. NOT EXISTS tests whether rows exist and avoids this particular NOT IN NULL trap. These quantified forms are PostgreSQL semantics; SQLite does not implement ANY/ALL syntax in the lab.

Exercise: Member IDs are 1, 2, 3 and non-NULL Borrow IDs are 1, 1, 2. Which Member survives NOT EXISTS?

Worked answer. Only Member 3. Duplicating Borrow ID 1 does not change whether a matching row exists.

quiz.question: In Sale, what is Hue’s total after WHERE amount >= 30?
quiz.explanation: The row with amount=10 is filtered out, leaving 30+90=120. WHERE filters individual rows before GROUP BY computes SUM, so the sale of 10 does not contribute.
